articles.title_orig: Pope Leo returns to what is expected to be a national party in his second homeland of Peru
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo returns to what is expected to be a national party in his second homeland of Peru
articles.content_orig:
Lee el artículo en español
Riding on horseback to visit the most isolated Andean areas of his community, distributing food amid the Covid-19 pandemic, or wearing rubber boots in the water and mud of floods: this is how many Peruvians remember the man who is now Pope Leo XIV.
Robert Prevost was in the trenches and alongside his people during Peru’s most difficult moments, and many of these memories will likely be front of mind among the public as they welcome the pope on his visit to his adopted homeland on Wednesday.
Pope Leo arrived in Callao city, near Lima, to a hero’s welcome with spectators at the airport waving flags and cheering as he stepped out of his plane and waved to the crowd. He was received by high-ranking officials including President Keiko Fujimori and Foreign Minister Carlos Espá.
The pope’s trip to Peru, which will include visits to Lima, Cusco and Chiclayo, is widely seen as a homecoming for a pontiff who knows the country in depth and is a Peruvian citizen. In fact, he will receive a new Peruvian ID card that will list Chiclayo as his address.
A young Prevost first arrived in the South American country as a missionary in 1985. The years that followed shaped his leadership style, which would later lead him to become the successor to the late Pope Francis.
“I think he was heroic in many ways; he risked becoming ill. We lost 11 priests and a bishop emeritus during that time,” Father José Del Rosario recalls of the most difficult days of the pandemic.
Padre Robert, as he is known in Spanish in Peru, traveled more than 700 kilometers (435 miles) from Chiclayo to the Diocese of Callao, a province bordering the capital, Lima, where he served as apostolic administrator.
“He came every two weeks in his little car; he came alone in a simple pickup truck,” explained Del Rosario, parish priest and rector of the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Mount Carmel of La Legua, who worked closely with the then-bishop.
Pope! Amigo! Peruvians remember the young American priest who became pope
Prevost distributed food and everything needed by a population that lived under lockdown for months, while also offering spiritual guidance during the crisis.
“He gave us a lot of hope and cared for our people, a man who was very close to the people … and also very humble,” Del Rosario added.
Peru recorded more than 219,000 deaths , according to Johns Hopkins University figures, and one of the highest coronavirus mortality rates in the world. In Lima, and especially in the regions, terrifying scenes unfolded outside hospitals, with sick people collapsing in the street due to the shortage of oxygen, one of the key tools for treating the virus.
In Chiclayo, Bishop Prevost launched a fundraising campaign to purchase an oxygen plant. Together with Caritas Chiclayo, the bishop appealed to authorities and sectors of civil society and managed to raise more than US$380,000 for not just one but two oxygen plants.
Janinna Sesa, former director of Caritas Chiclayo, worked with the bishop for eight years, including during the pandemic, the flooding caused by the coastal El Niño in 2017, and Cyclone Yaku in 2023.
“We were always on the front lines, especially during disasters like the coastal El Niño phenomenon. He was the person who put on his boots and waded into the water; he helped people. He was very approachable and very kind,” Sesa told CNN.
Before leaving for Rome in 2023, after the late Pope Francis appointed him prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops and president of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America, Bishop Prevost also led appeals for aid for the more than 10,000 people affected by flooding caused by Cyclone Yaku in the north of the country.
“I ask you to be generous; I ask you to open your hearts so that we can help one another and move forward, as we have done in other times of crisis,” Prevost said in a video while standing in the water in the district of Illimo, in the Lambayeque region.
Examine the power held by popes throughout history
The assistance and response led by Prevost in the face of the massive arrival of Venezuelan migrants in 2018 was comprehensive and had a different vision from that of the country’s other regions.
Peru received more than 1.6 million Venezuelans through November 2025, the second-highest number in the region after Colombia. More than 20,000 of them passed through Chiclayo, and more than 3,500 families settled in the region, according to figures from the Commission for Human Mobility and Human Trafficking of the Diocese of Chiclayo. Prevost also promoted this commission to assist migrants and combat human trafficking.
First American pope marks July 4 on migrant island with plea for ‘compassion and generosity’
“The migration flow descended upon us, with thousands of migrants out on the streets, sleeping there, and the parishes serving as shelters,” Sesa recalled.
Father Robert was concerned not only with providing food and collecting clothing, blankets, and medicine, but also with building the San Vicente de Paúl village, which took them in at Puerto Etén.
“His simplicity, the peace he conveys, that serenity Monsignor Prevost had when listening to people — I still see it in Pope Leo XIV…. He welcomed us with such warmth, with so much love,” Lisbeth Díaz, a Venezuelan resident of Chiclayo and member of the Commission for Human Mobility and Human Trafficking, told CNN.
Prevost prioritized regularizing their legal status so they could work and integrate into society.
Prevost created spaces for dialogue and encouraged many people to raise their voices to denounce abuses during the internal conflict the country experienced beginning in the 1980s and to openly discuss the social reality during the authoritarian regime of the late President Alberto Fujimori in the 1990s.
At the Augustinian mission in Trujillo, the current pontiff and his seminarians traveled through towns and parishes in Andean areas, staging dramatizations that reflected the violence faced by peasants to encourage conversations that would help heal the trauma and pain they had suffered.
Prevost also participated in collecting signatures for the creation of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), which investigated the violence between 1980 and 2000 and human rights abuses, particularly in rural Peru. Trujillo and the parishes led by the current pontiff collected the largest number of signatures.
Leo XIV is a pope forged in Peru. The nearly two decades he spent in the land he adopted as his own profoundly shaped his ministry and set him on the path to the papacy. As a bishop, Prevost was a pastor close to his flock, and at the Vatican, one of his closest collaborators is the Reverend Edgard Rimaycuna, a native of Chiclayo.
His work in South America and his leadership of the Order of Saint Augustine caught the attention of Pope Francis, who first appointed him bishop of Chiclayo and later brought him to Rome, where he went on to hold one of the most important positions in the Vatican and also became a cardinal. This made him a candidate in the 2025 conclave.
Pope Leo presides at biggest Mass of his papacy in Buenos Aires, drawing 2.5 million crowd
In the past, the election of an American pope was considered impossible, given that the College of Cardinals did not wish to associate the papacy with the dominant political and cultural power. However, the cardinals who voted for Cardinal Robert Prevost in the 2025 conclave did not see him simply as a candidate from the United States.
His experience in Peru garnered broad consensus among the cardinals, who chose a bishop with roots in Latin America — someone who speaks Spanish fluently and is attuned to the concerns of the people of that continent.
The pope’s visit to Peru will be an opportunity for the Peruvian people to welcome Padre Robert back to the adopted country that shaped him — and that he shaped deeply as well.

articles.title_orig: ‘The world we know is over’ without urgent climate action, leaders tell Cop31
articles.title_zh: ‘The world we know is over’ without urgent climate action, leaders tell Cop31
articles.content_orig:
Marshall Islands president warns of worsening floods as UN chief calls for a windfall tax on oil and gas firms
Failure to provide an overwhelming response to the climate crisis means “the world we know is over”, the president of the embattled Marshall Islands has warned, as dozens of leaders gathered in Turkey for the Cop31 climate summit.
Hilda Heine, one of a handful of Pacific Island leaders to make an impassioned speech at Cop31 on Wednesday, told other heads of state that overshooting the 1.5C Paris temperature target would mean waves eating away their shores and floods that destroy towns, schools and hospitals.
She described seeing bright, lush coral beneath the water of her home island in July that had been bleached white just months later.
“It’s time to wake up,” said Heine. “Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over.”
Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, also called out governments who had “not tried hard enough” to curb emissions since the Paris agreement.
“The UN tells us that, even if every pledge is delivered, we are heading for 2.6 degrees,” she said. “On current policies, 2.8 degrees is where we will end up.
“Let me be plain: overshoot is not a new target. It is a debt, a debt of heat, borrowed against our children’s future. And it must be repaid.”
The opening of the summit of international leaders, on day three of Cop31, saw impassioned speeches interspersed with vigorous displays of Turkish music and dancing.
António Guterres, the UN secretary general, blamed a deceitful fossil fuel industry and countries that “keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5C”. His speech – a salvo aimed at boosting the talks – was one of the last Guterres, a vocal climate advocate, will deliver as secretary general before he stands down next month.
“We need an extraordinary acceleration,” Guterres said. “Our planet is heating up. The clock is winding down. It’s make or bake time.
“Fossil fuels must go the way of the dinosaurs,” he added. “And that won’t happen on its own. The dinosaurs did not have a lobby – fossil fuels do.”
Guterres said oil and gas companies had distorted science and delayed action on the climate crisis, and called for a windfall tax on their bumper profits they have made from the Iran war. “It’s time to kick the habit and end the fossil-fuel addiction,” he said, to applause. “It’s time for governments to tax these windfall profits and use them to help vulnerable countries recover. Polluters must pay.”
Unusually, Turkey is co-hosting Cop with Australia, with the leaders of both countries, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Anthony Albanese respectively, each praising the partnership.
Erdoğan said he wants Cop31 to be remembered as a turning point in the climate crisis and called on countries to act, rather than just make promises. “Every minute we fail to meet the targets in the Paris agreement, the risks and costs we face continue to grow,” the Turkish president said. However, on Monday, away from the conference hall, ​​Erdoğan celebrated the discovery of two new oilfields with an estimated in-situ potential of 135m barrels.
In her speech before world leaders, Heine said every new oil well drilled and every piece of coal extracted was a threat to her country’s future. Without naming any individual oil or gas producer, she added: “The discovery of new fossil fuel resources is not something to celebrate but something to fear.”
Albanese said the conference was a “historic moment” for Australia. The country is one of the world’s biggest exporters of coal and liquified gas. Albanese said governments had a “solemn responsibility” to act on the climate crisis, but he was criticised for failing to mention fossil fuels in his speech.
The gathering of leaders was relatively threadbare. While 91 national leaders attended, according to the UN, major figures such as Donald Trump of the US and Xi Jinping of China were absent. Perhaps tellingly, some other leaders who declined to attend, including the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, are instead heading to Ireland for a conference on AI.
Almost every country at Cop31 is lagging in cutting emissions, with insufficient finance for the nations most vulnerable to extreme heat, floods, fires and other climate-fuelled calamities.
Although the world is barrelling past the 1.5C limit and is entering the teeth of one of the strongest El Niño events in history , there is little sign that the talks will feature any further progress on phasing out planet-heating fossil fuels.
“I’m getting a feeling of panic from around here, from the science community,” said Bill Hare, a climate scientist and chief executive of Climate Analytics, who described fraught conversations with rainforest and cryosphere scientists. “The mood is gradually darkening among scientists. In fact, people talk about feeling as though things have gone backwards.”
Small island nations face an existential threat from rising sea levels and are some of the countries most exposed to catastrophe when global heating shoots past 1.5C. The UN Environment Programme has found that such overshoot is now inevitable, and warned that its effects on icy regions will be so calamitous it should be kept as brief and low as possible.
Other world leaders stressed the urgency of this moment of multiple crises and the need for multilateralism to finally deliver. Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova, the president of North Macedonia, said: “We are the first generation to fully understand the consequences of our choices – and perhaps the last with time to change course. Future generations will live with the consequences of our decisions.”
Nataša Pirc Musar, the president of Slovenia, said: “If we cannot agree that human dignity and respect for nature must be at the heart of our decisions then, frankly, what is left to unite us?”

articles.title_orig: Renters in an unassuming state got slammed with the biggest rent hike in America after everyone moved there
articles.title_zh: Renters in an unassuming state got slammed with the biggest rent hike in America after everyone moved there
articles.content_orig:
Southern hospitality is coming with a steeper price tag.
Tenants in South Carolina have watched their housing bills climb faster than anywhere else in the nation, with the state’s median gross rent rocketing 19.2% in just two years, according to a new analysis.
The typical South Carolina renter forked over $1,395 a month in 2025, up from $1,170 in 2023, home warranty firm Cinch Home Services found after digging through American Community Survey figures the Census Bureau published on Oct. 29.
That surge nearly doubles the 10.7% jump renters saw nationwide over the same stretch.
Delaware landed a close second at 18.9%, trailed by South Dakota at 18.2%, North Dakota at 16.9% and Idaho at 16.4%.
So what’s driving the Palmetto State squeeze? It boils down to a flood of newcomers and not nearly enough places to put them.
South Carolina grew faster than any other state between July 2024 and July 2025, with its population swelling 1.5%, according to Census estimates.
“South Carolina experienced a population increase of 3.33% in two years, when comparing 2023 and 2025 population estimates, which is more than double the national change of 1.49%,” Doug Hollingsworth, senior content manager at Cinch Home Services, told The Post.
U-Haul also crowned it the nation’s top destination for net movers, and the jobs are following the crowds. The state notched the country’s largest percentage gain in payroll employment in the year through May 2025, adding 62,500 positions.
“People who are attracted to the sunshine, new employment opportunities and coastal living could be opting to move to South Carolina, as opposed to neighboring states, North Carolina or Georgia, where median rent is higher,” Hollingsworth said.
Builders have been playing catch-up for years. A 2023 study by state lawmakers and SC Housing pinned the shortage on rapid growth plus lingering underbuilding from the Great Recession, noting South Carolina’s population expanded 14% from 2010 to 2022, roughly twice the national pace.
The pain lands hardest on working families. University of South Carolina research economist Joseph Von Nessen found “about 90% of South Carolina’s lower-income households are estimated to be housing-cost burdened” in a statewide study.
Cinch’s numbers reveal a broader shake-up as well, with bargain states getting hammered while pricey ones barely budge. Hawaii posted the smallest increase of all, a modest 3.6%, though its $2,009 median still ranks second-highest in the country.
“Notably, the states with the lowest starting rents have often seen the sharpest increases, while already-expensive states like Hawaii and Colorado have seen the smallest rise,” a Cinch spokesperson said. “This suggests renters in more affordable states are rapidly losing that affordability advantage.”
New Yorkers aren’t off the hook either. Long Island’s Suffolk County saw the steepest climb of any large county in America, with median rent soaring 22.4% to $2,503. The Bronx clocked in fifth at 13.5%.
There may be a sliver of good news for South Carolina tenants. Apartment List tracked asking rents across the state moving less than 1% in either direction during 2025, while vacancies rose in most metros as new construction outpaced demand. The Census tally captures every renter, including those on existing leases, and folds in utility costs, so it reflects what households are actually paying rather than fresh listings.

articles.title_orig: Scoop: Inside Bessent's Situation Room confrontation with Lutnick over China chip security
articles.title_zh: Scoop: Inside Bessent's Situation Room confrontation with Lutnick over China chip security
articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent challenged Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over his department’s reluctance to label Nvidia customer Megaspeed a possible national security threat in a Situation Room confrontation last week that illustrates the tension inside the Trump administration over Chinese access to Nvidia’s advanced chips, two people familiar with the matter told CNN.
Trump officials have long harbored concerns that Megaspeed has circumvented US law and funneled advanced chips into China — a prospect that Treasury staffers argued should land it on Commerce’s so-called entity list of China-connected companies that could pose national security risks. But the issue gathered newfound attention and importance in recent days when Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a Megaspeed employee suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Senior Trump officials, including Lutnick, also were briefed months ago about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive who the intelligence community suspected of being a Chinese spy, people familiar with the matter said.
But despite those warnings, Commerce has so far refused to put Megaspeed on the entity list, the people said.
Confronted on it by Bessent last Thursday, Lutnick did not immediately commit to taking any specific action, they said.
Axios first reported the Situation Room confrontation.
Megaspeed is a Singapore-based company that was originally incorporated in 2015 as a Chinese video game developer called 7Road International. But in the three years since Alice Huang became director and the company changed its name, it has become one of the largest buyers of Nvidia chips in Asia , purchasing more than $4 billion worth of its semiconductors, by some analyst estimates.
Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing and said it is a “compliant and legal company.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the allegations that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy “groundless speculation and an attempt to smear and malign China.”
The entity list represents one of the US’s most significant tools for preventing American firms from selling their products to foreign companies and organizations. But adding Megaspeed to the list could also risk inflaming tensions with China amid Trump’s efforts to manage the US’ trade relationship with the fellow superpower. The Commerce Department hasn’t added any company to the list in more than a year.
Representatives for the Treasury and Commerce departments did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

articles.title_orig: Michel Houellebecq, French Writer, Is Investigated Over Anti-Muslim Remarks
articles.title_zh: Michel Houellebecq, French Writer, Is Investigated Over Anti-Muslim Remarks
articles.content_orig:
France’s cities are burning. For weeks, their populace has been terrorized by so-called protesters, who are smashing store windows, lighting cultural landmarks on fire, and assaulting citizens who stand up to them.
And yet the French legal system is spending its time charging writers for having an opinion about such behavior.
On Nov. 10, iconic French novelist Michel Houellebecq was charged with hate speech for comments made four years ago in a 2022 interview with Front Populaire in which he criticized Islam and expressed concerns about mass immigration into France.
It’s a disgusting inversion of justice — and an indication that a nation being torn apart from within is more concerned with thought crimes of its citizens than the actions of hooligans intent on destroying civilization itself.
The supposed hate incident involves mere words — including Houellebecq’s expressed fear that “when entire territories come under Islamist control … [violent] acts of resistance will take place.”
The author lives in Paris, where one in five residents was an immigrant as of 2023.
He went on to argue that “the wish of the population with French roots” is “for the violence to decrease, for [Muslim immigrants] to respect the law and people. Or, another good solution, for them to leave.”
Rather than debate or rebut, the Union of Mosques of France and the Orwellian-named Movement Against Racism and for Friendship Between Peoples slapped Houellebecq with a legal complaint. They went as far as to name the interviewer and the director of the magazine Houellebecq’s comments appeared in as defendants in their complaint.
They’re accusing him of “inciting violence” by expressing his opinions, but perhaps nobody knows better what having actual violence incited against oneself feels like than Houellebecq.
In 2015, he published a novel called “Submission,” a fictional account of France electing a Muslim president who slowly unleashes radical political and social transformation on the nation.
Subscribe to our daily Post Opinion newsletter!
The book coincidentally came out just a day after the Charlie Hebdo attack in Paris, where 12 employees of a satirical magazine which had caricatured Muhammad were massacred in their office, including one of Houellebecq’s friends.
The implication — that being even humorously critical of Islam could result in violent retribution — was clear enough to force Houellebecq into hiding, suspending his book tour and leaving his home in Paris. He was even ultimately given police protection.
But now, for sharing his opinion, a judge in Nanterre just charged Houellebecq with “complicity in incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence” — the same man who had to go into hiding under threat of violence by the exact group that he supposedly endangered.
Houellebecq’s lawyers told Le Monde that the “[incriminating] remarks have no dimension of incitement, not even implicitly” and that Houellebecq “[regrets] the increasing judicialization of intellectual debate.”
They also aptly added that “a prophet of doom does not wish for disaster.”
France ought to be ashamed of itself, not just for criminalizing the thoughts of a popular public intellectual, but for doing so against the backdrop of absolute anarchy across the nation.
For weeks on end, the country has been terrorized by chaos agents fashioning themselves as protesters, many of them from immigrant backgrounds themselves, who have caused an excess of €1 billion in damages to insured property. A historical city hall in Limoges was even destroyed by an arsonist’s fire.
On Oct. 17 alone, more than 1,000 police officers were injured and nearly 2,500 businesses were damaged. One agitator in Marseille attacked a woman who tried to stop teenagers from smashing a bus shelter — by hitting her in the face with flames from an aerosol can ignited with a lighter.
The courts should be overflowing with assailants and arsonists, but instead they have turned their attention to policing the interviews of public intellectuals.
In France, it seems it’s a greater crime to criticize immigration — or, god forbid, Islam — than to destroy cities and terrorize civilians.
The man who defends his nation’s spirit and integrity is treated as a greater threat than the man who burns that culture to the ground.

articles.title_orig: Spain: Housing crisis prompts first general strike in 14 years
articles.title_zh: Spain: Housing crisis prompts first general strike in 14 years
articles.content_orig:
Authorities in Spain say that despite pouring rain, some 120,000 citizens took to the streets of the capital, Madrid, on Wednesday evening after millions of striking workers brought Europe's fourth-largest economy to a standstill under the motto "Salaries. Housing. Prices" in the country's first general strike in 14 years earlier in the day.
The massive turnout came in response to housing shortages and unbearably high rents.
City officials in Barcelona said 55,000 people attended evening marches there as they walked behind a huge banner reading "Live. Not just survive." Housing activists in the city said the turnout was far larger, claiming that 400,000 had hit the streets.
As has been the case in other demonstrations across the Europea of late , peaceful protests later gave way to small groups of marauding young men who smashed storefront windows along Barcelona's main shopping street. They also set fire to dumpsters and shot fireworks at police when they arrived.
Earlier on Wednesday, workers across Spain gathered en masse, marching and setting up picket lines despite stormy weather in many areas of the country.
Symbolized by the eviction and death of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal in Madrid earlier this year, the crisis has also prompted a snap election set for November 29.
The government of left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez attempted to pass legislation to ease the plight of renters, but was blocked in parliament by opposition parties. Lacking the power to get legislation passed, Sanchez called the early vote in hopes of shoring up more support.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Sanchez's government did end up approving two extraordinary decrees introducing measures similar to the housing reforms rejected by parliament.
"We won't stop until we transform this country's housing model from top to bottom so that houses are for living instead of being at the service of the [landlord] minority," said Alicia del Rio, spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants' Union.
While most of the protests were peaceful, strikers in front of Madrid's Mercamadrid wholesale market said police had used pepper spray on the crowd, prompting at least 13 people to seek medical attention.
Some airlines later reported disruptions to flights in and out of Spain as some airport and airline workers participated in the strike.
The country has a deficit of about 750,000 homes, which is set ​to grow to more than a million by 2028, according to estimates from the central bank.
With fewer and fewer individuals and families able to buy a home, the number of renters in the country has risen sharply. According to Spain's youth council, the average rent is €1,176 ($1,315). This is equivalent to 99% of the average young person's salary.
The general strike came a day after rail workers launched a strike over two major deadly train crashes this year, making decrepit infrastructure another major issue in the upcoming parliamentary elections.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Spain's government supported Wednesday's strike, saying it was staged "in favor of rights" rather than against anyone. Sources close to Sanchez inner circle have gone so far as to say it is "against the opposition."
Alberto Nunez Feijoo, leader of the conservative People’s Party (PP), had a different take, saying if it was indeed "a strike against the opposition," it was "an absurdity the likes of which does not exist in any other European Union country."
Although the UGT labor union — one of the strike organizers — and Sanchez's socialist PSOE party are two separate institutions, they share a historic founder in Pablo Iglesias Posse.
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Nicole Ris, reporting for DW in Madrid, followed the strike closely as it unfolded on Wednesday, saying earlier:
Here in Madrid, apparently, lots of people are still showing up for work, and people I know have clearly said they will not go on strike as they don't see much sense in it — although they all suffer under the cost of living crisis and the housing crisis.
There is also debate about this strike being an "election strike" that could benefit the current government.
"I'm not taking part in this. It's nonsense. The government is supporting it because they hope they'll get enough votes on the 29th so they can carry on," a doorman in Madrid told me.
The government supports the strike, claiming it is being held "in favor of rights" rather than against anyone. Sources close to Sanchez's inner circle have gone so far as to say it is "against the opposition," according to the media here.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO could draw record retail buyers, Vanda Research says
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO could draw record retail buyers, Vanda Research says
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Everyday investors could pour a record $250 million into Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) shares on its first day of trading, according to Vanda Research.
The estimate, which would be more than double the $118 million in net retail buying the first day of SpaceX's ( SPCX ) June listing, hinges on a surge in derivatives trading tied to Anthropic's yet-to-be-listed shares on crypto exchange Hyperliquid.
Trading volume in this Anthropic-linked instrument reached a record $270 million on Tuesday, nearly triple last week's daily volumes, according to analysis from Vanda strategist Viraj Patel.
Vanda found that retail stock trading activity on the opening days of recent IPOs, including SpaceX, was roughly five times the peak daily trading volume in their pre-IPO derivatives. Based on Anthropic's Tuesday perpetual futures trading activity, the assessment would suggest $250 million in net buying on the company's planned listing day next week.
The projection comes with considerable caveats. The perpetual futures tied to Anthropic represent a speculative gauge of investor enthusiasm, and patterns from previous IPOs may not repeat.
Anthropic is targeting a valuation of $1.4 trillion, below the $2 trillion market value previously discussed, as the AI industry has faced headwinds from rising borrowing costs, hedge fund deleveraging, and political backlash over data center construction.
Anthropic is also planning a retail investor allocation of up to 20%, to be distributed through online brokerages, including US-based Charles Schwab ( SCHW ), Fidelity, Morgan Stanley's E-Trade, Robinhood ( HOOD ), and SoFi ( SOFI ).

articles.title_orig: Google Voice appears to finally be working on RCS support
articles.title_zh: Google Voice appears to finally be working on RCS support
articles.content_orig:
It might finally be happening. A new Google Voice update plants seeds of RCS support, though the exact details remain unclear.
About APK Insight: In this “APK Insight” post, we’ve decompiled the latest version of an application that Google uploaded to the Play Store. When we decompile these files (called APKs, in the case of Android apps), we’re able to see various lines of code within that hint at possible future features. Keep in mind that Google may or may not ever ship these features, and our interpretation of what they are may be imperfect. We’ll try to enable those that are closer to being finished, however, to show you how they’ll look in case that they do ship. With that in mind, read on.
Google Voice is an invaluable tool for accessing one phone number across a host of different devices, but to say it’s becoming less impactful without support for RCS is a bit of an understatement. Now that virtually every Android phone and iPhone supports the new messaging experience, Google Voice is less useful both for business and consumer users.
But that seems to be changing.
Google Voice for Android version 2026.11.01.1014278023 doesn’t enable RCS, but it does, for the first time, actually hint that the functionality might be on its way. In a teardown of the app, one simple string stands out:
That points to a new send button used for RCS messages rather than SMS. Google Messages similarly changes its send button to differentiate between the two standards.
This update contains a host of other new strings around images, videos, and more, but none of them are directly tied to RCS support.
The folks over at Android Authority dug up some other tidbits about RCS including an “RCS chat preference” toggle and various RCS actions and messages. But, again, nothing is live just yet, and there’s no word on when it might arrive, if ever.
Google has been championing RCS support for over a decade now, so it’s long past due for Voice, a long-running Google product, to get on board. While the tidbits in this update don’t serve as any confirmation RCS if coming to Voice, it’s the most exciting update on the matter in years.

articles.title_orig: Vessel renewal incentive policy in China: Potential greenhouse gas reduction impact and opportunities for improvement - International Council on Clean Transportation
articles.title_zh: Vessel renewal incentive policy in China: Potential greenhouse gas reduction impact and opportunities for improvement - International Council on Clean Transportation
articles.content_orig:
November 11, 2026 | By: Zhihang Meng, Hae Jeong Cho, Yuanrong Zhou, Gabriel Hillman Alvarez, Jakob Schmidt
Maritime shipping plays a key role in China’s national freight sector, accounting for over 50% of transportation activity in 2024. Decarbonization of this sector at a rate in line with the government’s goal to achieve carbon neutrality before 2060 will require the large-scale application of ships fueled by low- and zero-carbon fuels.
China introduced policies in 2024 to promote the scrapping and renewal of old ships, which offer shipowners tiered subsidies to renew older ships before their mandatory retirement dates, with greater support for new/clean energy vessels (NCEVs). However, the policy does not specify which fuels NCEVs must use.
This paper estimates the potential impact of the retire-and-renew (RNR) policy on fleet renewal and greenhouse gas emissions in China’s coastal fleet. Using the Vessel Economic Guidance and Assessment (VEGA) model and Polaris, a shipping emissions projection model, we estimated fleet renewal and greenhouse gas emissions from 2025 to 2050 under the existing RNR policy design and two alternative scenarios.

Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) has delivered stellar gains to investors in 2026, but the past few months have been quite forgettable.
Shares of the memory specialist have retreated 40% from the 52-week high reached on June 25. The broader sell-off in artificial intelligence (AI) stocks , driven by concerns about the sustainability of aggressive infrastructure spending amid rising borrowing costs from high interest rates, has weighed heavily on Micron lately.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
However, this isn't the first time that Micron stock has been caught up in a broader market sell-off. Let's see what happened the last time there was a steep sell-off in Micron's shares.
Image source: Getty Images.
There was a meltdown in technology stocks early last year when President Donald Trump announced tariffs on imports of goods into the U.S. The tariffs created panic among investors, driven by the belief that higher costs of goods due to import taxes were likely to hurt demand for various products.
There were reports that even Micron had to impose a surcharge on some of its products to offset the impact of tariffs. The fear of the tariffs' potential impact on Micron and other semiconductor companies' sales led to a big pullback in tech stocks. The Nasdaq Composite index lost nearly 20% of its value in just two and a half months, between early February and late April last year. Micron stock shed 30% of its value during this period.
However, Micron went on a remarkable bull run following this pullback. Shares of the company have skyrocketed by 830% since the beginning of May 2025 until now. This stunning rally has been fueled by Micron's healthy revenue and earnings growth, driven by a favorable memory market in which demand has significantly outpaced supply.
MU Revenue (TTM) data by YCharts
The good news for Micron investors is that the memory market's dynamics will remain in the company's favor. As such, I won't be surprised to see Micron stock going on another massive rally over the next couple of years, just like what happened after its 2025 sell-off.
Memory demand is poised to outstrip supply for the foreseeable future. Micron's peer SK Hynix (NASDAQ:SKHY) recently noted that it expects the memory market to remain supply-constrained until 2030. The South Korean memory giant points out that solid demand from AI data centers and emerging applications, such as humanoid robots, will be a tailwind for the market.
Additionally, SK Hynix notes that the new memory factories will take time to come online. As it turns out, more than half of SK Hynix's production capacity for 2027 and 2028 is already booked. Even Samsung estimates it won't be able to meet memory demand until 2028.
It is worth noting that Samsung and SK Hynix control 63% of the global dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) market, according to Counterpoint Research. Meanwhile, they control 47% of the NAND flash market. Micron, on the other hand, has a 24% share of DRAM, while its NAND flash share is 15%. Even Micron management remarked on the previous earnings call that memory and storage supply will tighten in 2027 and 2028.
Not surprisingly, Micron expects fiscal 2027 to be "even better" following a terrific fiscal 2026. Micron's fiscal 2026 ended on Sept. 3, and the company posted a 9x increase in adjusted earnings per share (EPS) to $75.52. The EPS estimates for the next couple of fiscal years point to durable growth in Micron's bottom line.
MU EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts
Also, the chart above indicates that analysts have been gradually raising their EPS estimates, which isn't surprising given tight supply conditions. Assuming Micron's EPS jumps to $207.76 in fiscal 2028 and it trades at even 10 times earnings at that time, in line with its current price-to-earnings ratio, the stock could soar to $2,078.
That implies a 172% jump from current levels, suggesting investors can buy a potential multibagger at an attractive valuation following Micron's recent pullback.

articles.title_orig: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
articles.title_zh: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
articles.content_orig:
Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day.
Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion.
However, both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon.
Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team said that this round of talks - the first since February - "was one of the hardest."
"I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion," he said. But he added that he felt "good momentum" and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible.
Comments by Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky were less conciliatory. "Right now... a lot depends on Ukraine, on the position of the US, and on whether Europe comes to its senses," he said.
After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - President Donald Trump's son-in-law - would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky.
The meetings in Abu Dhabi had been framed as centred around the "security architecture" of Europe.
For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member.
For Moscow, a reworked "security framework" is likely to include a limit to the influence of Nato in eastern Europe - a central concern for the Kremlin since the alliance's eastward expansion.
Earlier this week Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while the Kremlin's Medinsky said the world needed a "new" and "fair" security system.
That framework would serve as "a new Yalta and Potsdam", Medinsky said, referring to the 1940s summits in which the victorious Allied powers carved up post-war Europe into spheres of influence.
Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.
Representatives of Britain, Nato and various EU countries were also in Abu Dhabi and met with US and Ukrainian negotiators, but the Kremlin - with whom the EU does not officially communicate - said its delegation had not had any contact with them.
Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.
Many - particularly in eastern Europe - feel their security is linked to that of Ukraine. Agreements cannot be implemented "if no consensus can be reached among Nato members," a German government spokesperson said on Wednesday.
Kushner said the US was keen to bring the Europeans on board and said that getting them "added to the format" would be on the agenda for his talks with Putin.
There is also disagreement on whether discussions on a future security framework should be preceded by a ceasefire, as the Europeans and Kyiv would want, or whether the fighting only stops after an agreement has been reached, as the Kremlin has insisted.
Any agreement on a peacetime security framework, however, is contingent on the war ending, Kushner noted. But that cannot occur "until there's an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues," he added.
Since talks began last year, a core obstacle to any settlement has been Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia. Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are essential to its security.
Moscow, meanwhile, has never backed down from its demand that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds. "Every inch" of land would be "returned to Russia one way or another", Medinsky said.
Kushner acknowledged that the territorial question remained the hardest, while Zelensky's chief of staff and negotiator Kyrylo Budanov refused to be drawn on whether Russia was still demanding a Ukrainian withdrawal from the region.
Later, Budanov admitted the talks had been "tough" and that Ukraine's priority was to ensure Russia could not attack it again.
"These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex," Kushner said. "The reality is there is no trust right now between the sides and that is to be expected after a conflict like this."

Publisher Grindstone and developer Games Farm have announced Conan: The Black Pyramid , a roguelite action RPG “where sword and sworcery meets cosmic horror.” It supports two-player online cooperative play, and will launch for PC via Steam in 2027.
Here is an overview of the game, via its Steam page :
The Black Pyramid calls to warriors across time. Conan has answered.
Conan: The Black Pyramid is an action roguelite RPG where sword and sorcery meets cosmic horror. Fight alone or with a friend in two-player online cooperative play. Shape your build with every run, turn chance to your advantage, and return with new ways to challenge the darkness.
Step Into the World of Conan—And Beyond
Explore the distant lands of Robert E. Howard’s shared universe and take control of such iconic heroes as Conan, Solomon Kane, Dark Agnes, and more. Descend into eldritch chambers of the Black Pyramid, a mysterious and dangerous place that defies the logic of space and time. Confront the shadows of the champions themselves and piece together the dark secrets of their past.
Choose your own path through the shifting labyrinth of ancient ruins, ravaged kingdoms and occult halls ripped from different eras of time. Slay nightmarish monsters, savage beasts and bloodthirsty fanatics, and face off against challenging bosses that guard every layer of the Black Pyramid.
Every run presents new routes, new combat possibilities and new story events that move you closer to learning the truth: who summoned you here?
Show No Mercy to Your Foes
Choose from five distinct characters and weave crushing melee blows, precise swordplay, ranged gunfire and magical attacks into powerful combos. Dodge away from danger and stagger enemies with precisely timed parries to unleash brutal executions, or wear them down with dangerous status effects. Switch weapons and relics to adapt to every combat situation and outsmart your opponents.
Discover multiple Warrior Memories for every character, each with their unique combination of weapons and abilities that drastically change the playstyle. Define your build with ancient artifacts that grant new devastating effects, introduce new combat mechanics, or save you from a fatal blow. Combine them with upgradable Combat Masteries to create your own version of the unstoppable champion. Become even stronger with every attempt as you level up your heroes and unlock permanent upgrades with Wakestones.
As you search the Pyramid for perfect items for your build, you collect dice that increase your chances of better loot. Add more dice to your result and unlock additional rewards now, or save them for later when the stakes are higher.
Fight the nightmares of the Pyramid alone or with a friend in 2-player online co-op. Share the journey, earn individual rewards and keep your progression. Experiment with different characters and build combinations to truly dominate the foe, side by side.

articles.title_orig: Column | Powerful new weight-loss drug may also ease knee pain, major study finds
articles.title_zh: Column | Powerful new weight-loss drug may also ease knee pain, major study finds
articles.content_orig:
Eli Lilly and Co. (NYSE: LLY ) on Wednesday presented new clinical data showing the lasting benefits of a dual-drug approach for active psoriatic arthritis.
Detailed 52-week results indicate sustained and enhanced efficacy when combining two specific therapies, offering a positive outlook for patients managing multiple health conditions .
The recent data originates from the TOGETHER-PsA Phase 3b open-label clinical trial.
During this study, researchers assessed the concomitant administration of Taltz (ixekizumab) and Zepbound, or tirzepatide. The trial directly compared this combined regimen against the administration of Taltz on its own.
Read Also: Eli Lilly 'Deserves' Stock Upside: Analyst
The composite outcome of psoriatic arthritis disease activity (ACR50) plus at least 10% weight reduction was achieved at Week 52 by 39.2% of the combination arm and 1.7% of the Taltz-alone arm, compared with 31.7% and 0.8%, respectively, at Week 36.
85.7% of combination patients and 6.7% of monotherapy patients achieved at least 10% weight reduction at one year.
Lilly reported that ACR50 responses began separating between the arms as early as Week 4, before clinically meaningful weight loss was observed.
Participants taking Taltz and Zepbound together maintained their initial health gains. In many cases, the patients showed further improved outcomes as they progressed through Week 52 of the trial.
The combination therapy delivered these sustained improvements across several critical health metrics.
The clinical team observed continued progress in overall disease activity and crucial metabolic measures. Additionally, the trial recorded ongoing advancements in various patient-reported outcomes over the course of the year.
These comprehensive 52-week findings build heavily upon the trial's earlier achievements. As previously reported by the company, the Taltz and Zepbound combination already met the primary endpoint of the study at 36 weeks.
Minimal disease activity was achieved at Week 52 by 28.2% of the combination arm and 13.6% of the monotherapy arm.
The dual therapy also achieved all key secondary endpoints at that 36-week threshold.
During this earlier phase, the combination treatment demonstrated statistically significant superiority when compared directly to the Taltz-only regimen.

articles.title_orig: Pakistani TV Anchor Fatally Shot at Home
articles.title_zh: Pakistani TV Anchor Fatally Shot at Home
articles.content_orig:
Popular Pakistani TV anchor Rabia Ahsan was found shot dead inside her home, and the investigation into what happened has taken a surprising turn. The 41-year-old journalist was found Sunday in the bedroom of her home in Rawalpindi, according to The Indian Express . Ahsan was a mother of two daughters and hosted “Muqabil,” a current affairs program on 92 News HD.
Ahsan’s sister reportedly heard a gunshot and rushed into the bedroom. She found Ahsan on the floor and saw her husband, Ahsan Tahir, holding a pistol, according to the first information report described by CNBC-TV18 . Police recovered a .30-bore pistol and ammunition as investigators began examining the scene.
Tahir was taken into custody after the shooting. A domestic worker told investigators that Tahir said the gun had fired accidentally, according to Dawn . Police have not publicly determined whether the shooting was accidental or intentional. A court later granted police custody of Tahir as the investigation continued.
The case then took another turn. Ahsan’s brother, Khurram Ahmed, who initially filed the complaint, said he wanted to withdraw it because he believed his sister’s death was accidental, The Indian Express reported . Police, however, are continuing to investigate what happened.
Pakistan’s first lady, Aseefa Bhutto-Zardari, also called for a thorough and impartial investigation. She said the case deserves serious attention and accountability and stressed that women should be able to live and work without fearing for their lives, according to NDTV .

Artificial intelligence giant Nvidia is facing investor scrutiny due to concerns about the company's future amid its internal investigation into CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife in a statement on Sunday, in which he also said he had fallen short of his responsibilities to the company and said he would cooperate with the investigation.
Nvidia's board of directors initiated an independent probe into the matter, saying that while it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised, the probe will examine all available information.
The controversy has prompted some firms to alter their assessments of the company's shares, as Baird issued a rare downgrade of Nvidia stock – cutting the AI giant's rating to "neutral" because of a lack of visibility into 2027 data center spending, possible demand softness and uncertainty over Huang's tenure.

articles.title_orig: Big Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.
articles.title_zh: Big Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.
articles.content_orig:
The last few years have seen significant debate over the widespread use of AI-powered tools in game development and the responsible disclosure of that usage to players. That debate has exploded into a full-blown controversy in the indie game development space this week, as Big Walk developer House House has publicly and belatedly disclosed minimal AI use in its popular co-operative puzzle exploration game.
This particular controversy has been brewing behind the scenes for months, as judges and jury members for the prestigious Independent Games Festival Awards discussed the issue in private discussion groups. But the debate started to break into public view on Monday when 19 members of the 50-plus-member jury released a signed statement outlining a stance “declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity.”
Noting “a significant increase in the number of submitted games developer with generative AI tools,” the group of jurors called out AI’s ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms in rejecting tools whose use, they said, is still “not a foregone conclusion in our industry.”
The jurors also urged the IGF as a whole to “adopt a strong anti-AI policy for future years that disallows games containing any AI-generated work.”
Although the jurors’ statement didn’t name any specific games, by Tuesday morning, one critical darling in particular was increasingly being noted as a central part of the debate. In a statement provided to Aftermath (and added to the game’s FAQ page shortly thereafter), developer House House admitted publicly that “LLMs were used sparingly” near the end of Big Walk ‘s development “to help work through some difficult technical challenges and bugs.”
That limited AI use—which House House says represents “well under 0.1% of Big Walk ‘s code—stemmed in part from a thorny Unity engine bug that was slowing the game down with “infinite length” shadows during some game situations. After consulting with a Unity engineer who determined a fix “wasn’t possible,” House House said it consulted an LLM chatbot, which suggested a possible fix that the developers “had to modify… extensively” into the 10 lines of code that ended up in the final game ( At least one social media user says the bug was indeed fixable with significant human effort, though).
House House said it didn’t disclose this LLM usage for Big Walk ‘s Steam release earlier this year because Valve “does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage.” Indeed, Valve’s AI disclosure form for developers specifically notes that it is concerned with AI-generated content, not “efficiency gains” from “modern game development environments [that] have AI powered tools built into them.”
The IGF Awards make no such distinction for AI usage, however, which led House House to mention its AI-assisted bug fix in submitting the game for awards consideration. A version of that disclosure is being made public now because “it has become a matter of public interest,” House House said.
“This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal,” House House wrote. “We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalization of this technology, or its treatment as ‘inevitable.’ We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologize that Big Walk ’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.”
Learning of House House’s AI disclosure was particularly painful for some IGF judges who had previously felt a special connection to Big Walk . In a blog post discussing his feelings , IGF jurist Austin Walker called the game “an achievement” that was “remarkable” and “beautiful,” featuring puzzles that “capture a range of play that is largely abandoned by the digital form.” Fellow jurist Damon Reece shared in a blog post that the game is “seriously special to me” and that it gave him “a profound and powerful emotional reaction to being in a space that felt like home.”
But when it comes to IGF awards consideration, Walker and Reece were among those who said that even minimal use of AI tools overrode that deep and abiding respect for the work itself.
“We have our hands on the lever here,” Reece wrote. “This is pain that has to happen [emphasis in original] to try and steer our culture away from this. We need to choose to speak loudly and clearly on this, to prioritize human creativity and labour, to tell the culture and the world that this is unacceptable to us. To do otherwise is rank cowardice.”
This isn’t the first time AI usage has noticeably affected game award judging. Last year, the Indie Game Awards (which are completely separate from the IGF Awards) rescinded awards for Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 after the developers admitted that some in-game textures were made using AI tools (these were later patched out).
“The Indie Game Awards have a hard stance on the use of gen AI throughout the nomination process and during the ceremony itself,” they said at the time.
Since House House’s public disclosure, the anti-AI contingent of IGF judges has found plenty of support from disappointed Big Walk fans and industry observers. In the last few days, the game’s Steam page has been bombed with over 400 negative reviews, though Steam’s anti-review-bomb tools seem to be limiting the impact on the game’s overall “Very Positive” reception there.
But others feel House House’s relatively minimal use of AI here is being blown out of proportion. They say it’s important to differentiate between games that use LLMs as a last-resort technical fix, for instance, and others that lean heavily on AI to generate the bulk of their art, music, or the core of the game engine itself.
IGF judge Liz Ryerson wrote on social media that she didn’t find House House’s AI use to be personally disqualifying for the awards and that “the fact that many acted like there aren’t any levels to this and it’s all the same is bothersome to me.”
“To feel like someone gets punished a lot more for transparency about a smaller level of fuckup vs. just not even attempting to be honest or transparent at all is what bothers me,” she wrote.
Steam Hype staff writer and prolific Steam curator Dominic Tarason also pushed back against the idea that “House House need to be memory-holed and their work never spoken of again” as a “penalty for touching the Forbidden Device.” He said he considers Big Walk “very mildly compromised art” that is still “absolutely, unquestionably art and very human.”
“They spent years on that work of art,” Tarason added . “They asked a chatbot for two minutes how to fix a bug. That’s a ‘That’s lame, don’t do that again’ failing. … Some of you are acting like they’ve been convicted of high crimes against humanity, to be sealed away in the darkest oubliette until not even bones remain.”
But some have argued that using AI to fix a bug rather than hiring an expert to figure it out did make the game’s development at least a bit less human than it could have been. “House House aren’t laying off developers to replace them with Claude, and I’m sure they would be firmly against the mere thought of doing this, but we can also clearly see how their actions are part of the same problem,” AI researcher Mike Cook wrote on his blog .
Still, game developer, author, and professor Brendan Keogh wrote that he thinks “an extreme zero tolerance of any [generative AI] is ultimately counterproductive now. [There’s] a lot of anger at devs that feel deeply conflicted enough about their glorified Google search to disclose it, and [that is] encouraging those using it to actually steal labor to hide that use.”
As time goes on and AI tools are increasingly used in the building of major game engines , it may become increasingly difficult for anti-AI absolutists to avoid every game that has been touched by even a hint of LLM-generated code (if that use is even disclosed in the first place). articles.title_orig: American Airlines brings fresh food back to NY-Chicago first class for first time since 2019
articles.title_zh: American Airlines brings fresh food back to NY-Chicago first class for first time since 2019
articles.content_orig:
American Airlines is bringing back light bites and mini-meals in domestic first class on flights of 700–899 miles, according to aviation watchdog JonNYC , starting with New York–Chicago. Flights that currently offer a snack basket would get something more substantial.
This is a very good change. A flight can take up much of your afternoon without crossing American’s 900-mile meal threshold, especially when you include getting to the airport, boarding, and a connection. A small meal makes first class more worthwhile.
JonNYC reports that American Airlines is bringing back light bites and mini-meals on 700–899-mile domestic first class flights, starting on NYC/ORD.
American used to have a service between a basket of packaged snacks and a full meal. Before the pandemic, shorter flights could get something plated that would tide you over.
I covered the May 2015 improvements that replaced the afternoon basket of wrapped sandwiches, cookies, and bananas with snacks presented on china, with a proper napkin and flatware. Flights of 700–899 miles got warm nuts and these plated snacks. Examples included:
In 2016 I reported plans for plated morning items , including yogurt and breakfast cake. And my 2018 menu coverage included Lite Bites cheeses with cracked black pepper cheddar, cave-aged cheddar, Appalachian Tomme, and smoked Gouda.
American’s mainline standard is a snack basket on 500–899-mile flights during meal times, with meals starting in the 900-mile range.
United actually raised its meal threshold from 800 to 900 miles in January 2024 . American would be moving in the other direction, offering something more substantial on flights where Delta and United generally hand out snacks.
Alaska is still the standard to beat. They already feed passengers on shorter flights, and I’ve found their domestic first class food better than competitors’ .
New York–Chicago is an obvious place to start. New York LaGuardia–O’Hare is about 730 miles, and New York JFK–O’Hare about 740. An expansion might include:
American also used to have meal “exception markets” : shorter routes that got meals for competitive reasons. My January 2020 service guide listed Chicago–Dallas, Chicago–Boston, Chicago–New York, Los Angeles–Denver, and LaGuardia–Atlanta, among others.
I like a broad 700–899-mile rule better than making customers depend on whether their particular city pair merits an exception, though the exception markets got real meals and some were even shorter like Chicago–Washington National at just 612 miles which still wouldn’ qualify for a lite bite under this distance band.
This does mean more work for flight attendants. Individual food service means preparation, distribution, and clearing, with less time to do it on a shorter flight. American is also adding first class seats to some of its aircraft.
The airline’s product turnaround has been surprising, and surprisingly fast. They’ve introduced new business class suites, improved regional cabins and internet, upgraded coffee, and put money into lounges. They’re also reversing years of bad product decisions , including plans to bring back seatback screens and add more extra legroom coach seats.
The food improvements reach coach, too. American introduced Goldfish, Tate’s cookies, and a better snack mix this fall . They’ve improved food for sale , with a refreshed cheese plate and better snack boxes. Those are things passengers encounter on an ordinary domestic trip.
However there’s still work to be done.
Their returning coach food reservation program , announced with an initial Dallas–Fort Worth–Los Angeles test, should help passengers get the item they actually want. Mostly, though, I like that American seems to be loading enough food that there’s still something left when the cart reaches my aisle.
American has now announced the return of lite bites, with options including:
There will be two options onboard a given flight, with choices rotating “throughout the year.”

Note … ORD-DEN already gets full meals on AA, as it’s the one exception route that has never went away.
In my opinion, this is the type of change that AA needs to be doing. It’s one thing to match Delta and United but those airlines have already done what AA is matching so AA “premium” is looked at as “matching” vs finding ways to provide their own premium offering unique to AA (for now) where AA gets the credit for incrementally approving service levels across the industry, not just catching up.
This is what Delta was so good at in the 2010s. –Very small incremental improvements that really weren’t ever much (but marketed as being the best thing since the introduction of alcohol to airlines) but they were over and above competitors and they’d get “premium” credit for improving the customer experience even though Delta lagged (and still does in a number of areas) in “premium” vs competitors.
It’s the claiming your own “premium” narrative that AA needs to be focused on vs “catching up” in my opinion
@Drew Gary did a good article on that exact topic https://viewfromthewing.com/american-airlines-meal-rule-has-no-exceptions-except-one-route-tied-to-an-airport-that-closed-in-1995/
Now THIS is healthy competition… adding new amenities to stand out among its foes… good on you, American Airlines. I’ll say, was booked on WN for NYC-Chicago, but they failed me, and AA saved me, so… yeah… operational reliability matters, too, folks.
The press release actually contains items that look like real food.  Not just a cheese plate (although I’m sure that will often be what’s available).  Most importantly it shows AA understands it needs to compete in the main HNWI markets – NY, Chicago, LA.  This is a very positive sign.
While I miss “exception markets” (e.g., prior to the pandemic, DCA-ORD got *full* meals in first, not “light bites”), this is a very positive change that would make me shift business from UA to AA on sectors like ORD-LGA.
Notably, this sweeps in DCA to most of FL (MCO and south).  MIA barely made the threshold, PBI didn’t, and I genuinely don’t know about FLL.
It’s nice to see them make an effort after years upon years of absolute neglect.  While these changes are nice,  let’s see how the flight attendants act.  I’m sure they’ll be pissed because it requires a small iota of work from them instead of keeping the jumpseat from floating away.
Air Canada somehow manages to offer a hot breakfast on every single flight with a business class cabin, regardless of segment length, and yet US carriers sometimes say they can’t even do a beverage service in Y or a full meal in F on routes below 900 miles…
Lite Bites were also served on CLT-BOS, which is 727 miles. One of the few reasons I would intentionally connect at CLT pre-pandemic.  This restoration is most welcomed.
And yes, there had better be warm nuts with these restored Lite Bites.
Obese Americans can’t survive a 2 hour flight without gorging themselves on mediocre warmed airline food.

articles.title_orig: Hundreds of Schools in Italy Are Evacuated as More Bomb Threats Rattle Europe
articles.title_zh: Hundreds of Schools in Italy Are Evacuated as More Bomb Threats Rattle Europe
articles.content_orig:
Some 6,300 schools across Italy and more than 700 in Scotland and Northern Ireland have received bomb threats, according to local authorities.
In Italy a number of buildings were evacuated as a precaution but Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said checks so far had not indicated any evidence of "concrete danger".
"These reports appear rather linked to a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern," she said on Facebook.
Scotland's education secretary Mairi McAllan said there was no risk to the public and specialist cyber-crime officers were working to identify the source of the messages. In Northern Ireland education officials told schools to remain open unless otherwise advised by police.
It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.
"As a parent and as a constituency MSP I understand just how concerning this will be for parents, for pupils, for carers and for school staff," McAllan said.
Scottish police had earlier said that the warnings were "immediately assessed" as hoaxes. However some local authorities confirmed that some schools had been evacuated.
"Our advice is that there is no requirement to evacuate schools or keep children away from education based solely on the content of the emails," Police Scotland said.
Italian officials said a single email appeared to have been sent on Wednesday to the inboxes of 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 state schools, and private schools were unaffected.
The message, said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan", caused alarm in many schools.
The BBC has seen the email sent to Scottish schools which appeared to have similar wording, and also referenced the name Mikhail Andropov, although as leader of a "Red Owl" project.
Italy's Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said the incidents involving Italian schools were probably a "cyber-attack, not a genuine risk", adding that there appeared to be a clear strategy behind the rash of threats in across Europe targeting flights, supermarkets and even hospitals.
Italian airports along with airlines elsewhere in Europe were hit by a series of bomb hoaxes last week that prompted a series of scares, evacuations and widespread disruption.
Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.
On Wednesday one Milan headteacher, Anna Bertato, told Italian media she had checked the email address of the sender online: "It was already classified as spam by a student at a university in Taiwan."
Another Milan headteacher, Massimo Nunzio Barrella, told Adnkronos news agency that he had immediately realised the email was spam when it arrived in his inbox at 08:59 and he decided not to evacuate his school and reassured parents who phoned in.
"The text seemed almost comical," said Barrella, "it was like a message from Martians: 'We have come to annihilate you.' I even had a bit of a laugh."
Although many schools were initially evacuated on Wednesday, the alarm was quickly lifted, and pupils were allowed to return to class. Some parents decided to take their children home for the day, but the majority of schools in Milan did not send their pupils home.
Some 280 school head teachers had already received threats in recent days, according to Italian reports.
In a statement, the head of the central Umbria region Stefania Proietti said "checks conducted so far in Umbrian schools have proved negative, and law enforcement is working rapidly and carefully to verify each report".

articles.title_orig: Trump Officials Clashed Over Megaspeed, Firm at Heart of Nvidia Affair
articles.title_zh: Trump Officials Clashed Over Megaspeed, Firm at Heart of Nvidia Affair
articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent challenged Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over his department’s reluctance to label Nvidia customer Megaspeed a possible national security threat in a Situation Room confrontation last week that illustrates the tension inside the Trump administration over Chinese access to Nvidia’s advanced chips, two people familiar with the matter told CNN.
Trump officials have long harbored concerns that Megaspeed has circumvented US law and funneled advanced chips into China — a prospect that Treasury staffers argued should land it on Commerce’s so-called entity list of China-connected companies that could pose national security risks. But the issue gathered newfound attention and importance in recent days when Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with a Megaspeed employee suspected of being a Chinese spy.
Senior Trump officials, including Lutnick, also were briefed months ago about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive who the intelligence community suspected of being a Chinese spy, people familiar with the matter said.
But despite those warnings, Commerce has so far refused to put Megaspeed on the entity list, the people said.
Confronted on it by Bessent last Thursday, Lutnick did not immediately commit to taking any specific action, they said.
Axios first reported the Situation Room confrontation.
Megaspeed is a Singapore-based company that was originally incorporated in 2015 as a Chinese video game developer called 7Road International. But in the three years since Alice Huang became director and the company changed its name, it has become one of the largest buyers of Nvidia chips in Asia , purchasing more than $4 billion worth of its semiconductors, by some analyst estimates.
Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing and said it is a “compliant and legal company.” China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the allegations that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy “groundless speculation and an attempt to smear and malign China.”
The entity list represents one of the US’s most significant tools for preventing American firms from selling their products to foreign companies and organizations. But adding Megaspeed to the list could also risk inflaming tensions with China amid Trump’s efforts to manage the US’ trade relationship with the fellow superpower. The Commerce Department hasn’t added any company to the list in more than a year.
Representatives for the Treasury and Commerce departments did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

articles.title_orig: China select board deals with complicated issues
articles.title_zh: China select board deals with complicated issues
articles.content_orig:
China select board members had several complicated issues on their Nov. 2 agenda, not all ripe for decision. They decided three:
— Board members unanimously approved a new, less comprehensive proposal from Raegan LaRochelle to assist with developing China’s revised Tax Increment Financing (TIF) plan (see the Oct. 22 issue of The Town Line, p. 3 ). LaRochelle will receive $3,200 for about three weeks spent educating the select board and the public and working with them and Town Manager Rebecca Hapgood to identify town projects eligible for TIF funding. Her fee will come from the TIF account. — After discussion of the town’s partly-outdated Telecommunications Ordinance, board members unanimously accepted Harmoni Towers’ bond in the amount of $68,637.75. The bond is intended to cover the cost of removal when the tower the company has approval to build on Parmenter Hill becomes obsolete (see the Oct. 29 issue of The Town Line, p. 2 ). The bond amount did not have the professional engineer’s endorsement that the ordinance requires. Codes Officer Nicholas French said confirming removal cost estimates is “not what professional engineers do.” — By yet another unanimous vote, board members changed China’s HRA (Health Reimbursement Account) from the current administrator to Consumer Health Solutions, saving $470 and, Hapgood hopes, getting as good or better service.
The HRA is related to the town employees’ health insurance plan, topic of a quarter-hour discussion and no decision. The Maine Municipal Employees Health Trust currently offers five plans; China is enrolled in the middle one, in terms of employee costs and benefits. The town would save money by switching to a less generous plan.
Hapgood said with the HRA covering employees’ costs, like deductibles and co-pays, last year was the first year the town didn’t “make employees whole.”
She invited select board members to send her questions to be answered at the Nov. 16 board meeting. With open enrollment starting Nov. 15, she expects a decision on Nov. 16.
Another issue involving money and potential complications is dispatching emergency services. Currently, China uses the Kennebec Sheriff’s Office (KSO), which in turn uses the state system. This system, Select Board Chairman Brent Chesley said he learned at a meeting the previous week, is outdated, and the state won’t spend money to update it.
Therefore, KSO intends to switch to the City of Augusta’s dispatching service, at a higher cost.
Chesley was indignant about several aspects of the planned new system. Each town’s charge is based on a 1987 formula, 75 percent on population and 25 percent on call volume, which he said is contrary to state statute.
The formula also hurts China and Chelsea, two Kennebec County towns that contract for KSO patrols, Chesley said. Every time a KSO deputy calls in to check a license plate, China gets billed for a call.
Chesley was more indignant because he had learned that towns with their own dispatching service don’t pay the county anything. He said he asked at the meeting if there is a county service China doesn’t use, can the town be exempted from paying for it?
A final insult, he said, was when county officials proposed starting the new service – and billing for it – on April 1, instead of waiting for the towns’ new fiscal years to begin July 1.
The dispatch bill will be separate from the annual county tax bill, he said.
Also needing decision soon is whether to renew the contract for disposal of bulky waste and construction debris or to seek a new company. The current contract with Waste Management ends Dec. 31. Hapgood said Transfer Station Manager Thomas Maraggio is seeking prices from several services.
Board members heard of, but did not discuss, one more potential expense increase, for Delta Ambulance. The towns of Fairfield and Benton have notified Delta that they intend to stop using its service in February 2027. Delta officials will have to find some way to continue to pay bills without those two towns.
As the meeting ended, Hapgood reminded those present that all town departments will be closed Wednesday, Nov. 11, for the Veterans’ Day holiday; and Thursday and Friday, Nov. 26 and 27, for the Thanksgiving holiday.
The Nov. 16 select board meeting is scheduled for 6 p.m. in the town office meeting room.
